official_measurement_examples.name: Failure scenario not probability
official_measurement_examples.fact: Reservoir flood maps show where water may go in the unlikely event of reservoir or dam failure; the mapped extent is a consequence scenario, not a probability that failure will occur.

official_measurement_examples.name: Dry-day and wet-day separation
official_measurement_examples.fact: Environment Agency reservoir maps maintain separate dry-day and wet-day scenarios and these must not be collapsed into a single flood likelihood value.

official_measurement_examples.name: High-risk designation meaning
official_measurement_examples.fact: High-risk reservoir designation is based on whether uncontrolled release could endanger human life; it does not mean the dam is more likely to fail.

official_measurement_examples.name: Not-high-risk limitation
official_measurement_examples.fact: A not-high-risk designation does not mean no downstream damage or no regulatory duties; statutory reservoirs still retain registration, incident and emergency-plan requirements.

official_measurement_examples.name: Large raised reservoir threshold
official_measurement_examples.fact: Current England reservoir-safety guidance uses 25,000 cubic metres above ground level for a large raised reservoir; the 2026 reform programme must not be treated as already changing every current statutory threshold.

official_measurement_examples.name: Multiple reservoir effects
official_measurement_examples.fact: More than one reservoir can affect the same location; a single-reservoir extent cannot be assumed to represent all reservoir-flood scenarios at a site.

official_measurement_examples.name: Fluvial extent distinction
official_measurement_examples.fact: The maximum fluvial extent used in wet-day reservoir mapping is not the same as Flood Zone 2 or 3 in the Flood Map for Planning.

official_measurement_examples.name: Planning assessment limitation
official_measurement_examples.fact: Environment Agency guidance says reservoir maps should inform SFRA and FRA work but not be used in isolation; site safety, emergency planning and reservoir-owner impacts require proposal-specific assessment.

core_rules: reservoir flood extent is a failure-consequence scenario not failure probability
dry-day and wet-day reservoir scenarios must remain distinct
high-risk reservoir designation is consequence-to-life classification not likelihood of failure
not-high-risk does not mean no flood or damage risk
current statutory threshold must remain distinct from reform proposals
one reservoir extent does not represent all reservoirs affecting a location
reservoir wet-day fluvial extent is not Flood Zone 2 or 3
reservoir maps should not be used in isolation for planning decisions
reservoir safety compliance is not planning permission
planning permission is not reservoir-safety approval
reservoir owner/operator status does not establish parcel ownership
flood-map presence does not determine development yield
emergency planning and safe lifetime require proposal-specific evidence
future reform or research classification is not current designation
no parcel reservoir-flood clearance or Future Growth score may be promoted while recovery is parked
